title: Getting better with practice
keyIdea: Doing something again and again makes it easier. A first try is often wobbly, and that is normal. Each go teaches your hands and brain a little more, so a later try is neater. A little practice every day works better than one long go. Practise the tricky bit, and look back at your first try to see how far you have come.

kid: The first time you cut with scissors, the line is wobbly. That is fine. Everyone starts wobbly.
Have another go. And another. Each go, your hands learn a bit more. Soon the cut is neat. That is practice.
Practise a little every day. A short go on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday helps more than one very long go.
Find the tricky bit and practise that part. Then look at your first try. Look at your new try. You got better!
adult: This is part of the EYFS Characteristics of Effective Teaching and Learning. Active learning means children keep on trying when things are hard. Development Matters asks 3 and 4 year olds to keep going with a task, and Reception children to show resilience and perseverance. The ELG Fine Motor Skills asks them to use scissors, pencils and cutlery with growing skill. Cutting, name writing and pedalling all get better in ways a child can see.

Key words: practice (doing a skill again and again), first try, later try, the tricky bit, and little and often. Little and often is called spaced or distributed practice. Motor learning studies find it keeps a skill better than one long block of practice, called massed practice. With enough practice a skill becomes automatic: it takes less effort and less thinking.

Common mistakes: thinking some children are just born good, so practice does not matter; giving up after one wobbly go; practising only the easy parts; and cramming one long go, after which the skill slips. Be careful with praise. Praise the practice (you kept going and it got neater), not talent (you are so clever). Praise for talent can make children avoid hard things.

In the lab your child cuts a wiggly line three times and sees the cut get neater. They spot which try came after practice, race a little every day against one long go, and practise the wobbly S in a name. Then they fill a week of practice stars for a skill they choose. Every drag has a big button twin.

familyTip: Keep your child's first drawing, cutting or name writing with the date on it. After a few weeks of short daily goes, put the new try next to it and ask: 'What changed? What did you do to get better?'

visual.caption: First try or after practice? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: A cut line that zigzags off the dots
A cut line right on the dots
Letters that wobble up and down
Letters all the same size on the line
The ball goes in the hoop

lab.caption: Flagship lab: cut a line again and again, spot the later try, race little and often against one long go, and practise the tricky bit.

practice.prompt: Getting better with practice: your first go at cutting a line is wobbly. What is the best thing to do?
practice.hint: Think of the cutting lab. What happened to the line each time you had a go?
practice.explain: Have another go. Each go teaches your hands more, so the cut gets neater.

practice.prompt: You practise riding your bike for a short go each day. You do it for {n} days. How many short goes is that?
practice.hint: One short go each day. Count the days.
practice.explain: One go a day for {n} days is {n} short goes. Little and often helps the skill stick.

practice.prompt: Which helps you get better at writing your name?
choices: One very long go, then stop
practice.hint: Remember the race between the two plans in the lab.
practice.explain: A short go every day kept getting better. After one long go, the skill slipped back.

practice.prompt: Sam can write {n} letters neatly. He practises and gets 1 more letter neat. How many neat letters now?
practice.explain: {n} and 1 more is {=n+1}. Practising the tricky letter made one more neat.

pool.prompt: Some children are good at cutting. How did they get good?
pool.hint: Everyone starts wobbly. What made the lab cut get neater?
pool.explain: People who are good at something practised a lot. Nobody is born neat at cutting.

pool.prompt: Mia's M is neat, but her i is wobbly. What should she practise?
pool.hint: Practise the part that is still tricky.
pool.explain: The i is the tricky bit. The M is already neat, so practising it again helps less.

pool.prompt: Your first try and your tenth try at catching. Which is likely to be better?
pool.hint: Each go teaches your hands a little more.
pool.explain: The tenth try comes after nine goes of practice, so it is usually better.

pool.prompt: How can you see that you got better?
choices: Look at your first try next to a new try
Only look at other people's tries
pool.hint: Keep your first try so you can compare.
pool.explain: Putting a first try next to a new one shows how much your practice helped.

pool.prompt: Pedalling a bike used to be hard. Now it is easy. Why?
pool.hint: What did you do again and again?
pool.explain: It got easy because you kept practising. Your legs learned the skill.

pool.prompt: You put a sticker on the chart each day you practise. You practise for {n} days. How many stickers?
pool.explain: {n} days of practice means {n} stickers on the chart.

pool.prompt: Your cut was {n} steps away from the line on your first go. Practice made it 1 step closer. How many steps away is it now?
pool.hint: Closer means fewer steps away. Take 1 away from {n}.
pool.explain: {n} take away 1 is {=n-1}. Each go of practice brings the cut closer to the line.

pool.prompt: Your first go at a jigsaw is slow. What does that mean?
choices: It is new, and it gets faster with practice
Jigsaws are only for big children
pool.hint: A first go is often slow or wobbly. What happens with more goes?
pool.explain: Slow at first is normal for anything new. With practice it gets quicker and easier.
